feat(otp): pin mail-sourced OTPs to the sender's domain

Correlate the page requesting an OTP with the domain of the email the OTP
came from, so a phishing page on an unrelated domain cannot harvest a code.

- Mail extension: parse the From header and forward sender_domain in new_otp.
- Daemon: store sender_domain in the OTP slot and only serve a pinned code to
  a matching (or subdomain) host; include sender_domain in otp_available.
- Browser extension: when delivering otp_available, only target requesting
  tabs whose host matches the pinned sender domain.
- Codes from non-mail sources (Bluetooth/ANCS/mobile) stay unpinned and keep
  the previous behaviour.

feat(otp): derive sender domain from DKIM/Return-Path and match by eTLD+1

- Mail extension now reads raw headers (getFull) and prefers the DKIM d=
  signing domain, then Return-Path, then the From header, so the pinned
  domain is the validated sending domain rather than a spoofable display name.
- getFull is only fetched once an OTP candidate has been found, keeping normal
  mail cheap.
- Replace the directional subdomain matcher with a shared registrable-domain
  (eTLD+1) comparison in both the extension and the daemon, backed by a curated
  subset of the Public Suffix List for common country-code second-level domains.
  This matches apex <-> subdomain in both directions (accounts.google.com vs
  google.com) and handles amazon.co.uk-style domains correctly.

feat(otp): map known sender domains to their login domain

Add a small sender-domain alias table so services that email from a different
registrable domain than their login site still correlate. The first entry maps
facebookmail.com -> facebook.com; resolveSenderDomain canonicalizes the derived
domain through this table before it is sent to the daemon.
docs: add SECURITY.md

fix(otp): only pin mail OTPs to a server-validated DKIM domain

The From and Return-Path headers (and even a raw DKIM-Signature header) are
attacker-controlled, so falling back to them let a spoofed email pin an OTP to
an arbitrary domain. Instead, read the receiving server's Authentication-Results
header and only use a domain from a dkim=pass result (header.d, falling back to
header.i). When no signature passed, leave the OTP unpinned rather than trusting
a forgeable header.

fix(otp): use the real Public Suffix List for registrable-domain matching

The previous matcher used a hand-picked table of two-label suffixes. That was
correct for the entries it contained, but for any multi-part suffix missing from
it (e.g. com.cy) both 'evil.com.cy' and 'bank.com.cy' collapsed to 'com.cy' and
matched - the opposite of the intended fail-closed behaviour.

Replace the curated table with the full PSL (ICANN + private sections), generated
once into a shared data file and consumed by both the JS extension and the C++
daemon. Both sides implement the same prevailing-rule algorithm, including
wildcards (*.ck) and exceptions (!www.ck), and IDN rules are punycoded at
generation time so the runtime comparison stays ASCII-only.

Regeneration: node scripts/generate-psl.mjs /path/to/public_suffix_list.dat

feat(cli): subcommands for the flags that already exist

tether has grown a lot of flags, and people reach for 'tether devices'
before 'tether --list-devices'. This adds a subcommand for each, rewritten
into the flag it stands for before parsing, so there is still one parser
and every flag keeps working exactly as it did.

'tether bt <name>' maps to '--bt-<name>' by rule rather than by table, so
the Bluetooth flags cannot drift out of step with their subcommands.

The help output grows a Commands: section. A subcommand borrows the
description of the flag it stands for, matched on the long flag, so the
two lists cannot disagree.

headless: tetherd under systemd, with --status and --pending (#161)

* feat: run tetherd headless, under systemd, and drive it from the CLI

The daemon does not need a Wayland session, but until now there was no way
to see what it was doing or accept a pairing request without the GTK app,
and nothing shipped a unit to keep it running.

  --status   what the daemon is doing: devices, links, recent transfers
  --pending  the Wi-Fi pairing requests waiting, with their fingerprints

Both read the state_snapshot the GTK app already uses, and parse only the
first line of the reply so a broadcast arriving mid-request cannot turn into
a parse error.

A tetherd.service user unit comes with it. The distro packages install it
into /usr/lib/systemd/user; a portable build has no package to do that, so
'tether --install-service' writes a copy into ~/.config/systemd/user with
ExecStart pointed at wherever that build lives. Neither enables anything:
the unit is written, the commands that start it are printed, and the choice
stays with the user.

Spawning and systemd had to be taught about each other. A client starts
tetherd on its own when none is running, which leaves a daemon holding the
TCP listener that the unit then cannot bind, and it would restart into that
failure every RestartSec. So clients no longer spawn once the unit is
enabled, the unit takes over a daemon that was spawned before it, and the
start limit bounds what is left.

* feat(cli): finish the subcommand table, and two headless fixes

Now that both halves are on one branch, the three verbs held back from the
subcommand PR have flags to point at: status, pending and service.

The unit took over an already-running tetherd with 'pkill -x tetherd', which
matches the process name. A client spawns the daemon with argv[0] "tetherd",
but comm comes from the executed file, so an AppImage's daemon shows up as
the AppImage's own name and never matched. Match the command line instead.

The comments there described the takeover as a contended TCP listener. It is
not: ensure_single_instance() takes a flock before either server starts, and
the listener sets SO_REUSEPORT, so the port was never the thing in the way.

--install-service and --uninstall-service wrote and removed a unit whether or
not the machine has systemd, then printed systemctl commands that do not
exist there. Check for systemctl first and say so instead. The check lives in
the CLI so service.cpp stays a plain file writer its tests can drive without
systemd.

Add headless OCI container runtime support

Runs tetherd non-root in Docker, reusing the host's BlueZ/Avahi and a
private session bus/OBEX inside the container. CLI-driven only; no web
UI yet.

- TETHER_NO_AUTOSTART=1 stops the CLI from spawning a competing daemon
  when a supervisor (systemd or a container entrypoint) already owns it.
- TETHER_LOG_STDERR=1 keeps daemon logs on stderr instead of redirecting
  to the state-directory log file, for docker logs.
- XDG_DOWNLOAD_DIR, when absolute and nonempty, now takes precedence
  over the GLib/HOME download-directory lookup.
- Incoming Wi-Fi pairing no longer treats a missing/failed dialog
  helper as a rejection; it stays pending for explicit CLI approval.
  The dialog is now skipped only when neither WAYLAND_DISPLAY nor
  DISPLAY is set, so X11-only desktops keep the existing popup.
- The file-received callback records completed transfers independently
  of desktop notifier initialization.
- tether status rejects a reply whose command isn't state_snapshot, and
  reassembles a state_snapshot reply that arrives across multiple reads,
  bounded in both size and time so a stalled daemon fails fast instead
  of hanging the CLI.

Adds packaging/container/ (Dockerfile, entrypoint, healthcheck, Compose
example), docs/CONTAINER.md, a GitHub Actions build/smoke workflow, and
new tests: fixture binaries for container smoke testing, and a
tether_headless_test suite exercising the real daemon/CLI in isolated
homes.
